newsitem.title: USA: Storm threat in U.S. Gulf boosts Louisiana crudes.
newsitem.headline: Storm threat in U.S. Gulf boosts Louisiana crudes.

text.p: A growing storm front in the Gulf of Mexico triggered a price spike for sweet cash crude prices Thursday morning in U.S. market activity, traders said.

Outright prices gained on the NYMEX market as well, putting August West Texas Intermediate/Cushing 45 cents firmer at $20.05-15 a barrel, eliminating the September WTI premium. August/September spreads were out to 12-14 cents in favor of the second month on Wednesday.
Early on Thursday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center upgraded a weather disturbance to Tropical Storm Danny, causing refiners to scramble for barrels ahead of possible production disruptions.

Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James sold out to a 32 cents premium to the August WTI/Cushing, and may have been done at 35 cents over the marker, traders said. The storm-related gains pushed LLS values out some 10-15 cents from Wednesday.
Other talk had Midland/WTI sweets moving to a 18-23 cents discount to the benchmark, and Heavy Louisiana Sweet/Empire around 15-20 cents under WTI.
Traders said late deals on Wednesday saw LLS sell at 23 and 24 cents over the marker, with West Texas Sour/Midland done at a $1.17 discount to WTI.
WTS failed to budge from last deals, talked at a $1.15-20 discount to the marker, and Eugene Island at $1.20-25 under.
Sour crude rallying may have run its course pending further word on when Colombian Cano Limon production would resume.

Leftist rebel bombings have paralyzed the 300,000 barrel per day Cano Limon-Covenas pipeline since July 6, forcing force majeure declarations by Ecopetrol and by Cano Limon field operator Occidental Petroleum Corp.
WTI/Cushing Postings Plus sold at $1.98 and $1.99, moving out on the firmer August/September roll, traders said.
Traders also have kept close watch on the United Nations for possible word on when Iraqi oil sales restart. The sanctions committee is scheduled to meet later Thursday.

Earlier this week, Western diplomats on the sanctions panel said Iraq would likely be allowed to rollover only a small portion of first 90-day oil sales allotments of $1 billion to the second 90-day period, setting the stage for larger than expected oil volumes.

"There is a strange thing going on here. In the short-term there is more of a percieved tightness, but in the longer-term thereis plenty of oil, expecially if the Iraqis have to pump most of that $1 billion immediately," said a Gulf trader.

Traders still expected Iraqi crude back on the market in late July, but more likely in early August. U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan still must approve an aid distribution plan, then Iraq has to provide a pricing formula.
